newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. says Hebron deal stuck on mistrust not issues.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Hebron deal stuck on mistrust not issues.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk said in remarks published on Thursday that a lack of trust, rather than issues, was holding up an Israel-PLO deal on Palestinian self-rule for the West Bank town of Hebron.

"We are so close to an agreement on Hebron and yet still so far from it. There is very little -- in fact actually nothing -- to negotiate anymore," Indyk told aid workers on Wednesday night in remarks that the U.S. Embassy published on Thursday.
"What is at the core of the problem here between Israelis and Palestinians is a lack of trust and a lack of confidence in the intentions of each other," Indyk said.
Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) have failed in 10 weeks of U.S.-brokered talks to seal a deal under which Israel would hand over most of Hebron to PLO self-rule.

The handover, due last March, was delayed after a wave of Islamist suicide attacks killed scores in Israel. The deal was further delayed after Israeli voters elected right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in May.
Netanyahu has demanded security guarantees for the 400 Jewish settlers who live and study in the heart of Hebron.
The PLO has sought assurances that Netanyahu will not halt implementation of interim peace accords signed by Israel's previous centre-left government once the Hebron deal is done.

Indyk said Israel could not have confidence in Palestinian intentions without the "unending, unwavering commitment" of PLO security forces to fight against "terrorism". Indyk praised Palestinian police for cooperating in the arrest of radical Arab gunmen behind the killing of two Jewish settlers last week.

Indyk, restating U.S. President Bill Clinton's "real concern" over Israeli settlement activity, urged Israel to avoid actions or statements "which create the impression one side intends to pre-empt the outcome of the negotiations".

Netanyahu has come under international criticism for his moves to bolster Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza, seized by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war. Under interim peace deals, the fate of settlements is to be determined in "final status" talks that have yet to resume under Netanyahu.
